There was a little greek place I really liked. I think it went under new management. They remodeled the place to fit more tables. It does look nice but they also changed the business from a pay up front to a sit down waiter type of place. I detest restaurants with waitstaff for multiple reasons.

Anyway, I was in a hurry because I had to get to work. Fast forward to after I'm done eating. She saw that I was done, but she kept going to other tables. Passing right by me over and over again. I was not going to be late for work. She was in the middle of chatting with a group, working for those tips, and I walked up to her and told her I was leaving and I was paying right now. She got all apologetic and presented me with an ipad. So she is holding this ipad and I have to touch the greasy screen. Not only that but she is literally staring at the screen when I have to enter a tip.

Never went back.

One day I got off of work to find that my SO had left me. We had been texting then suddenly she stopped and when I got home, no one was there. She had an Iphone that was connected only to wifi, no cellular and she wasn't showing up anywhere on find my iphone.

I stayed out all night looking for her. I would be more worried but I kind of figured she had left me. The next day instead of going to work, I hung out in a McDonald's near my work all day and kept waiting for her to show up. Eventually she did. The little map indicator showed her hundreds of miles away in another state. That was the worst experience I had ever had at a restaurant.

Sorry for the delay on another one of these! I was planning on doing a basic command every week or so, but real life keeps getting in the way. Today I'll be going over the training of the hand targeting, which I personally use the word 'Touch' as a prompt. You can use whatever word you want as a verbal prompt, but I'll be referring to hand targeting as touch during this write-up. Here is a video of a dog performing the command.

Now, touch is an orientation command. What this means is that you have a way to position your dog wherever you need to when using this command. This can be used in many ways, such as getting your dog over to you, getting your dog's focus back on you, or even getting a fearful dog to move a bit. For example, I went to a university where I was taught how to train service dogs and was paired with a very anxious dog my second semester. If she seemed overwhelmed in a public place, I often used touch to get her to refocus on me and to get her to realize the situation wasn't that bad. My first semester I had a dog who was likely to completely forget I existed, and I used to touch in a similar way - to get her to realize that I needed her attention.

Training touch is a simple process. You start out placing your hand, with your palm outstretched, close to your dog's nose, with a treat tucked in between your hand and your thumb. The desired result is that your dog goes to get the treat, and touches their nose to your palm. When this happens, you can mark the moment and let your dog have the reward. Repeat this step about 6 times, but you can keep staying on this step until your dog gets it.

The next step would be to remove the lure part of training. You'll never be removing the physical prompt of your hand, so all you need to do for this step is not have the treat placed in your palm anymore. Now when you have your dog perform the behavior, you'll be rewarding using your other hand. From here, you'll move to variable reinforcement, which means you'll be rewarding randomly.

Throughout the training process, you'll want to make sure your dog can see your hand and that your hand isn't too far away from your dog's nose. Once you have moved on to a reliable command on variable reinforcement, you can start to move your hand farther away from your dog's face. If you want to advance even more, you can try placing your hand where your dog can not immediately see your hand and have them look for it.
